subject: Chem
title: Particles, atoms & bonding
sub: States of matter, atomic structure, bonding and structure, formulae, equations and moles
strategyIntro: Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences tests chemistry alongside biology and physics: a multiple-choice paper (40 questions, 45 min), a theory paper of structured questions, and a practical or alternative-to-practical paper. Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “effervescence” or “fizzing”, not “it reacts”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Equations: check every atom balances, and add state symbols when the question asks.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Colour changes need both colours: “blue to white”, not just “white”.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Saying ionic bonds “share” electrons. Ionic = transfer; covalent = share.
Writing “chlorine” when you mean the chloride ion, or “clear” when you mean “colourless”.
Calculations without units, or without the working shown.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords. Cards marked (Extended) are Supplement content.

flashcards.back: Particles closely packed in a regular arrangement; they vibrate about fixed positions. Fixed shape and fixed volume.
Particles close together in an irregular arrangement; they move around (slide past) each other. Fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
Particles far apart in a random arrangement, moving quickly in all directions. No fixed shape or volume; easily compressed.
Solid changes to liquid at the melting point. Energy is taken in to overcome the forces of attraction between particles.
Boiling happens throughout the liquid, at the boiling point only. Evaporation happens only at the surface, at temperatures below the boiling point.
Condensation: gas to liquid. Freezing: liquid to solid. Both give out energy to the surroundings.

flashcards.front: Flat section on a heating or cooling curve
flashcards.back: Temperature stays constant during a change of state, because the energy is going into (or coming from) changing the forces between particles, not changing their speed.
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their random movement.
Particles move faster. At constant pressure the gas expands (volume increases). In a fixed volume the pressure increases, because particles hit the walls harder and more often.
Gases with a lower Mr diffuse faster. Ammonia (Mr 17) diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride (Mr 36.5).
A substance made of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into anything simpler by chemical means.
A substance containing two or more different elements chemically combined (bonded) in a fixed proportion.
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined. It can be separated by physical methods.
Relative charges: +1, 0, −1. Relative masses: 1, 1, 1/1836 (negligible). Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are in shells.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. In a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Neutrons = mass number − proton number.
Atoms of the same element with the same proton number but a different number of neutrons (so a different mass number).

flashcards.front: Why isotopes react the same way
flashcards.back: They have the same number of electrons, arranged in the same electronic configuration. Chemical properties depend on electrons.
Shells fill in order: 2, then 8, then 8 (for the first 20 elements). Sodium (11) is 2,8,1; calcium (20) is 2,8,8,2.
Number of outer-shell electrons = group number (groups I–VII). Number of occupied shells = period number. Noble gases have a full outer shell.
Average mass of the isotopes, weighted by abundance. Chlorine: 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl gives (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = 35.5.
A charged particle, formed when an atom (or group of atoms) loses or gains electrons. Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions.

Between a metal and a non-metal. Electrons are transferred from metal atoms to non-metal atoms, and the oppositely charged ions attract. (Extended: a strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.)
A pair of electrons shared between two atoms, usually non-metals, so each atom gets a full outer shell.
High melting and boiling points; conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not when solid; often soluble in water.

flashcards.front: Why solid ionic compounds do not conduct
flashcards.back: The ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move. When molten or in solution the ions are free to move.
Low melting and boiling points; do not conduct electricity. (Extended: the forces between molecules are weak, even though the covalent bonds inside them are strong.)
Giant covalent structure: each carbon atom bonded to four others. Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct. Used in cutting tools.
Giant covalent structure: each carbon bonded to three others in layers. Layers slide (soft, slippery); one electron per atom is free to move, so it conducts. Used as a lubricant and for electrodes.
Giant covalent structure like diamond: each silicon bonded to four oxygens, each oxygen to two silicons. Hard, high melting point, does not conduct.
Electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The moving electrons let metals conduct; layers of ions can slide, so metals are malleable.
The number and type of each atom in one molecule, e.g. ethene is C₂H₄.
The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms in a compound, e.g. ethene C₂H₄ has empirical formula CH₂.
The average mass of the isotopes of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula. CO₂ = 12 + 16 + 16 = 44.
Same number of each type of atom on both sides. Change only the big numbers in front of formulae, never the small numbers inside them.
(s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous: dissolved in water.
Sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺. Balance the charges to get the formula, e.g. Al³⁺ and O²⁻ give Al₂O₃.
The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant). Moles = mass ÷ Mr.
One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) at room temperature and pressure. Volume = moles × 24.
Moles of solute per dm³ of solution: concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³). Divide cm³ by 1000 to get dm³.

quiz.q: Which describes the particles in a liquid?
options: Regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions
Close together, irregular arrangement, moving past each other
Far apart, random arrangement, moving quickly
Close together, regular arrangement, not moving at all
quiz.why: Liquid particles are still touching but are not in fixed positions, so they slide past each other. Particles in a solid always vibrate, so “not moving at all” is never right.

quiz.q: What happens to the temperature of a pure solid while it is melting?
quiz.why: During a change of state the energy taken in overcomes the forces between particles, so the temperature stays the same until all the solid has melted.

quiz.q: Which change of state gives out energy to the surroundings?
quiz.why: Condensation (gas to liquid) releases energy as particles come closer and attractions form. The other three take energy in.

quiz.q: A gas is heated inside a sealed container that cannot change size. What happens to its pressure, and why?
options: It increases: particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
It stays the same: the volume cannot change
It increases: the particles get bigger
quiz.why: Heating gives particles more kinetic energy. Faster particles collide with the walls more often and with more force, so pressure rises. Particles never change size.

quiz.q: (Extended) Cotton wool soaked in ammonia is put at one end of a long glass tube and cotton wool soaked in hydrogen chloride at the other. Where does the white ring of ammonium chloride form?
quiz.why: Ammonia (Mr 17) is lighter than hydrogen chloride (Mr 36.5), so it diffuses faster and travels further before the gases meet. The ring forms nearer the HCl end.

quiz.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
quiz.why: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23. The proton number is 11 (this is sodium).

quiz.q: Which of these is a compound?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide is carbon and oxygen chemically combined. Oxygen is an element; air and brass (an alloy) are mixtures.

quiz.q: What is the electronic configuration of chlorine (proton number 17)?
quiz.why: 17 electrons fill shells 2, then 8, then the remaining 7. Seven outer electrons puts chlorine in Group VII.

quiz.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes. How are their atoms different?
quiz.why: Both have 6 protons and 6 electrons. Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, carbon-12 has 6. Same electrons means same chemistry.

quiz.q: (Extended) Boron is 20% boron-10 and 80% boron-11. What is its relative atomic mass?
quiz.why: (20 × 10 + 80 × 11) ÷ 100 = (200 + 880) ÷ 100 = 10.8. The answer is nearer 11 because boron-11 is more common.

quiz.q: Which pair of elements forms an ionic compound?
quiz.why: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a non-metal. Sodium is the only metal here; the other pairs are non-metals that bond covalently.

quiz.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
options: It contains ions that can move
Each carbon atom forms four bonds
Some electrons are delocalised and free to move
quiz.why: Each carbon uses three electrons to bond, leaving one free to move along the layers. Graphite is a non-metal and has no ions.

quiz.q: Substance X melts at −95 °C and does not conduct electricity as a solid or a liquid. What type of structure does it have?
quiz.why: A very low melting point means weak forces between molecules. Ionic compounds conduct when molten, and giant structures have high melting points.

quiz.q: How many covalent bonds are there in one molecule of methane, CH₄?
quiz.why: Carbon has four outer electrons and shares one with each of four hydrogen atoms: four single bonds.

quiz.q: How does a magnesium atom become a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺?
quiz.why: Mg is 2,8,2. Losing the two outer electrons gives 2,8 (full outer shell) and a 2+ charge. Protons never change in a chemical reaction.

quiz.q: What is the relative formula mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
quiz.why: 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100. A common slip is to count only one oxygen (68).

quiz.q: Which is the correctly balanced equation for hydrogen burning in oxygen?
quiz.why: The product must be water, H₂O, and oxygen exists as O₂ molecules. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 4 H and 2 O on each side.

quiz.q: Aluminium ions are Al³⁺ and oxide ions are O²⁻. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
quiz.why: Two Al³⁺ give +6 and three O²⁻ give −6, so the charges cancel: Al₂O₃.

quiz.q: (Extended) How many moles are in 8.0 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH (Mr = 40)?
quiz.why: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 8.0 ÷ 40 = 0.20 mol. 5.0 comes from dividing the wrong way round.

quiz.q: (Extended) What volume does 0.50 mol of carbon dioxide occupy at room temperature and pressure?
quiz.why: Volume = moles × 24 dm³ = 0.50 × 24 = 12 dm³. Any gas, same rule.

examIntro: Theory-paper style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: State two differences between boiling and evaporation.
points: Boiling happens at one temperature (the boiling point); evaporation happens at any temperature below it
Boiling happens throughout the liquid (bubbles form); evaporation happens only at the surface
exam.note: Each point must describe both processes.

exam.q: A purple crystal of potassium manganate(VII) is placed at the bottom of a beaker of water. After an hour the purple colour has spread through the water. Explain this, and explain why it would spread faster in warm water.
points: The crystal dissolves and its particles spread out by diffusion
Particles move randomly / collide with water particles
Net movement from high concentration to low concentration
In warm water particles have more kinetic energy / move faster
So diffusion is faster

exam.q: Ice at −10 °C is heated steadily until it becomes steam at 110 °C. Describe and explain the shape of the temperature–time graph.
points: Temperature rises while it is solid ice
Graph is flat at 0 °C while the ice melts
Graph rises again while it is liquid water
Graph is flat at 100 °C while the water boils
On flat sections energy is used to overcome forces between particles, not to raise the temperature
Temperature rises again once it is all steam
exam.note: Any 5. Give the two temperatures of the flat sections.

points: Atoms of the same element / same number of protons
With different numbers of neutrons / different mass numbers

exam.q: Magnesium has proton number 12. For an atom of magnesium-24, state the number of protons, neutrons and electrons, and its electronic configuration.
points: 12 protons
12 neutrons (24 − 12)
12 electrons

exam.q: Iron filings and powdered sulfur are mixed, then the mixture is heated to make iron sulfide. Explain the differences between the mixture and the compound.
points: In the mixture the elements are not chemically combined; in the compound they are bonded
The mixture can be separated by physical means, e.g. a magnet attracts the iron
The compound can only be separated by a chemical reaction
The compound has a fixed composition; a mixture can have any proportions
Making the compound involves a chemical reaction with an energy change (it glows)
The compound has different properties from its elements, e.g. iron sulfide is not attracted to a magnet

exam.q: Sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. Explain why.
points: In the solid the ions are fixed in position / cannot move
When molten the ions are free to move (and carry the charge)
exam.note: Say “ions”, not “electrons”: electrons moving is a common wrong answer.

exam.q: Sodium is 2,8,1 and chlorine is 2,8,7. Describe how sodium and chlorine atoms form sodium chloride.
points: Sodium atom loses (transfers) one electron
Chlorine atom gains one electron
Forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
Both ions have a full outer shell (2,8 and 2,8,8)
Oppositely charged ions attract: ionic bond

exam.q: Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon. Explain how their structures lead to their different properties and uses.
points: Both are giant covalent structures of carbon atoms
In diamond each carbon is bonded to four others
So diamond is very hard and is used in cutting tools / drill tips
In graphite each carbon is bonded to three others, in layers
Weak forces between layers let them slide, so graphite is a lubricant / used in pencils
Graphite has free (delocalised) electrons so it conducts and is used for electrodes
Diamond has no free electrons so it does not conduct
exam.note: Any 6. Link each property to a structure point.

exam.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂. (Ar: Mg = 24, N = 14, O = 16)
points: Correct method: 24 + 2 × (14 + 3 × 16)
exam.note: Everything inside the bracket is doubled.

exam.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols.
points: Correct formulae: Mg, HCl, MgCl₂, H₂
Balanced: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
State symbols: Mg(s), HCl(aq), MgCl₂(aq), H₂(g)

exam.q: (Extended) 2.4 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure. (Ar: Mg = 24)
points: Moles of Mg = 2.4 ÷ 24
Mole ratio Mg : H₂ is 1 : 1, so 0.10 mol of H₂
Volume = 0.10 × 24
exam.note: Unit needed for the last mark.
